provenance.note: 1 - Medical Terminology Cardio Vascular FM1E 2026.pdf (Medical Terminology, Pr Hicham Benyoussef)

body.build_note: Built from the lecture slides. Slides that only show pictures are covered in outline. If your professor says something different, trust your professor.
exam_points: Decode: suffix first, then prefix, then combining form(s).
angi/o, vas/o, vascul/o = vessel.
arteri/o artery; ven/o and phleb/o vein; thromb/o clot; ather/o fatty plaque.
Endocardium (inner), myocardium (muscle), pericardium (around; visceral = epicardium).
Angina pectoris = ischaemic chest pain; MI = death of myocardial cells.
CAD: atheromatous coronary arteries.
CHF: heart cannot pump enough; cardiomegaly: enlarged heart.
Bradycardia slow; tachycardia fast; fibrillation quivering (defibrillate); asystole = no beat (CPR).
Vital signs: TPR + BP.
Troponin rises when myocardial cells die.
PTCA = coronary angioplasty; CABG = bypass graft.
Aspirin prevents platelet clumping; thrombolytics dissolve clots.

deeper.title: Why so many words for 'vessel'
deeper.html:
Medical vocabulary grew from both Greek and Latin: angi/o is Greek, vas/o and vascul/o are Latin, and they coexist in different terms (angiography, vasospasm, vascular). The same happens for vein: phleb/o (Greek, phlebitis) and ven/o (Latin, venous). Recognising both versions is what lets you read any cardiology report.

Source: the lecture's combining form tables.

deeper.title: Why the suffix changes everything
deeper.html:
The same root gives very different meanings depending on the suffix: cardi/o with -logy is a specialty, with -megaly an enlarged heart, with -myopathy a disease of the muscle, with -centesis a puncture. That is why the lecture insists on reading the suffix first: it tells you whether you are looking at a disease, a procedure or a description.

Source: the lecture's Medical Language Key.

provenance.note: 4 - Medical Terminology Endocrine system FM1E 2025.pdf (Medical Terminology, Pr Hicham Benyoussef)

body.build_note: Built from the lecture slides. Slides that only show pictures are covered in outline. If your professor says something different, trust your professor.
exam_points: Hormones: secreted by endocrine glands directly into the blood.
Homeostasis: home/o constant + -stasis control.
adren/o adrenal; gonad/o gonads (testic/o, ovari/o); pancreat/o islets; parathyroid/o; pineal/o; pituit/o; thym/o; thyr/o.
Pituitary controls the other glands, driven by hypothalamic neurohormones.
ACTH → adrenal cortex; TSH → thyroid; GH (somatotropic) → growth.
FSH, LH/ICSH → gonads (ovulation, sperm, testosterone).
Prolactin (lactogenic) → milk; MSH → melanin.
ADH (antidiuretic) → water retention; oxytocin → labour contractions, milk flow.
Melatonin → circadian sleep-wake cycle.
Glucagon raises, insulin lowers blood glucose.

deeper.title: Why the pituitary is called the master gland
deeper.html:
Most pituitary hormones end in -tropic (having an affinity for): each one targets another gland, such as the adrenal cortex (ACTH) or the thyroid (TSH). The pituitary itself answers to the hypothalamus, forming a chain that keeps hormone levels in balance. Reading the -tropic hormone names tells you exactly which gland each one drives.

Source: the lecture's pituitary slides.

deeper.title: Why ADH is 'anti-diuretic'
deeper.html:
Diuresis means increased urine production. ADH works against it by making the kidneys return water to the bloodstream, which concentrates the urine and supports blood pressure. The name, built from anti- + diuretic, states the function directly.

Source: the lecture's posterior lobe slide.

provenance.note: 3 - Medical Terminology GI FM1E 2025.pdf (Medical Terminology, Pr Hicham Benyoussef)

body.build_note: Built from the lecture slides. Slides that only show pictures are covered in outline. If your professor says something different, trust your professor.
exam_points: GI tract = alimentary canal, mouth to anus; accessory: liver, gallbladder, pancreas.
dent/o, odont/o teeth; gingiv/o gums; gloss/o, lingu/o tongue; or/o, stomat/o mouth.
sial/o, ptyal/o saliva: sialorrhea, ptyalism.
esophag/o-scope (instrument), -scopy (exam), -tomy (incision), -tome (cutting tool).
-emesis vomiting: hyperemesis, haematemesis.
-pepsia digestion (dyspepsia); -phagia swallowing (dysphagia, aerophagia); -orexia appetite (anorexia).
enter/o small intestine; col/o large intestine; rect/o rectum; an/o anus.
hepat/o liver; chol/e bile; cholecyst/o gallbladder; -lithiasis stones.
Peristalsis moves the bolus; chyme forms in the stomach.
carcin/oma = malignant epithelial tumour.

deeper.title: Why two roots for the same organ
deeper.html:
Greek and Latin both left their mark: tongue is gloss/o (Greek) and lingu/o (Latin), mouth is stomat/o (Greek) and or/o (Latin). Clinicians use both, often the Latin in everyday adjectives (oral, sublingual) and the Greek in disease names (stomatitis, glossitis). Knowing both pairs doubles the words you can decode.

Source: the lecture's oral cavity tables.

deeper.title: Why dys- turns up so often in digestion
deeper.html:
Dys- means bad, painful or difficult, and many digestive complaints are exactly that: difficult swallowing (dysphagia), difficult digestion (dyspepsia). Combined with the right suffix, one prefix names a whole family of symptoms, which is why suffix and prefix tables are worth memorising.

Source: the lecture's suffix table.

provenance.note: 6 - Terminology Immune system 2025.pdf (Medical Terminology, Pr Hicham Benyoussef)

body.build_note: Built from the lecture slides. Slides that only show pictures are covered in outline. If your professor says something different, trust your professor.
exam_points: Lymphatic functions: absorb fats (lacteals), remove waste, return lymph to veins.
Lymph path: capillaries → vessels (valves) → nodes → two ducts → veins at the neck.
Lymph nodes: lymphocytes destroy bacteria, viruses, malignant cells.
Allergist, immunologist, lymphologist, oncologist (onc = tumour).
Immune threats: pathogens, allergens, toxins, malignant cells.
Antigen = anything regarded as foreign; antibody binds and labels it.
B cells make antibodies (immunoglobulins).
Tolerance = acquired unresponsiveness to an antigen.
Autoimmune = antibodies against one's own tissues.
anti- against; leuko- white; erythro- red; oligo- few; pseudo- false.

deeper.title: Why lymph needs valves and nodes
deeper.html:
Lymph has no pump of its own; it is squeezed along by surrounding muscles and closing capillary cells. Valves stop it flowing back, and nodes act as checkpoints where lymphocytes can meet any bacteria, viruses or cancer cells carried from the tissues before the fluid returns to the blood.

Source: the lecture's lymphatic structure slides.

deeper.title: Why antibodies 'label' rather than kill
deeper.html:
An antibody on its own mostly neutralises and tags an antigen; the actual destruction is done by other immune cells that recognise the tag. That is why the lecture describes the antigen-antibody reaction as flagging a dangerous antigen so it can be recognised and destroyed.

Source: the lecture's antigen-antibody slide.

figure.caption: From tissues to veins, and antigen-antibody binding. Schematic drawn for this site.

provenance.note: 0 - Medical Terminology intro FM1E 2026.pdf (Medical Terminology, Pr Hicham Benyoussef)

body.build_note: Built from the lecture slides. Slides that only show pictures are covered in outline. If your professor says something different, trust your professor.
exam_points: Four word parts: root, combining form, suffix, prefix.
Root = basic meaning (body part); cannot stand alone.
Combining form = root + o.
Suffix at the end (procedure, condition); prefix at the start (location, time, number).
Decode from the suffix backwards.
Rule 1: root + vowel suffix; Rule 2: combining form + consonant suffix; Rule 3: combining form joins two roots.
-itis inflammation; -ectomy removal; -otomy incision; -ostomy opening; -plasty repair.
-rrhage bleeding; -rrhaphy suturing; -rrhea flow; -rrhexis rupture.
hyper- increased; hypo- decreased; dys- bad; eu- good.
Colours: cyan/o blue, erythr/o red, leuk/o white, melan/o black.
Symptom = felt (pain); sign = observed (fever); syndrome = set of both.

deeper.title: Why start decoding at the suffix
deeper.html:
The suffix usually tells you what kind of word you are dealing with: a disease (-itis, -osis), a procedure (-ectomy, -scopy) or a description (-al, -ic). Reading it first frames the rest: in 'gastroenteritis', -itis says inflammation, and the roots then say where (stomach and small intestine). Working backward is how the lecture recommends taking terms apart.

Source: the lecture's 'taking terms apart' slide.

deeper.title: Why the combining vowel exists
deeper.html:
Joining 'gastr' directly to 'dynia' would give an unpronounceable cluster. The combining vowel, usually o, makes the word easy to say. It is dropped before a vowel-initial suffix (gastritis), which is why the three rules of word building matter for spelling as well as meaning.

Source: the lecture's word root and combining form rules.

figure.caption: Pericardiectomy split into its parts. Schematic drawn for this site.
labels: Read from the suffix, then prefix, then root
= removal of part of the pericardium

provenance.note: 8 - Medical Terminology Musculo skeletal system FM1E 2025.pdf (Medical Terminology, Pr Hicham Benyoussef)

body.build_note: Built from the lecture slides. Slides that only show pictures are covered in outline. If your professor says something different, trust your professor.
exam_points: Skeletal functions: framework, protection, movement, calcium storage, blood formation (red marrow).
Long bone: epiphyses (spongy, red marrow), diaphysis (compact), medullary cavity (yellow marrow).
arthr/o joint; oste/o bone; chondr/o cartilage; burs/o bursa; ten/o tendon; spondyl/o vertebra; cost/o rib.
kyph/o hump; lord/o swayback; scoli/o curved; ankyl/o stiff.
Hydarthrosis = fluid in a joint; haemarthrosis = blood in a joint.
-penia deficiency (osteopenia); -desis fusion; -lysis freeing; -synthesis connection.
Auto- (self), allo- (same species), xeno- (other species) grafts.
Tetraplegia (4 limbs) vs paraplegia (legs).
Brachy- short, dolicho- long: brachydactyly.

deeper.title: Why bone marrow comes in two colours
deeper.html:
Red marrow is active blood-forming tissue, rich in developing blood cells, and sits in spongy bone at the ends of long bones. Yellow marrow is mostly fat and fills the shaft's medullary cavity. The distinction appears in the bone diagram and explains why bone marrow samples are taken from spongy bone.

Source: the lecture's skeletal structure slide.

deeper.title: Why graft prefixes matter
deeper.html:
Auto-, allo- and xeno- describe where tissue comes from, and that predicts rejection risk: an autograft is the patient's own and is not rejected, an allograft from another person needs matching, and a xenograft from another species is the most foreign. The prefixes carry clinical meaning, not just vocabulary.

Source: the lecture's prefix table.

provenance.note: 5 - Medical Terminology Nervous system FM1E 2025.pdf (Medical Terminology, Pr Hicham Benyoussef)

body.build_note: Built from the lecture slides. Slides that only show pictures are covered in outline. If your professor says something different, trust your professor.
exam_points: CNS = brain + spinal cord; PNS = 12 cranial + 31 spinal nerve pairs.
Meninges: dura (outer), arachnoid (middle), pia (inner).
CSF lies in the subarachnoid space; epidural space is outside the dura.
cerebr/o cerebrum; encephal/o brain; mening/o meninges; myel/o spinal cord or marrow; neur/o nerve; gli/o neuroglia.
-paresis partial paralysis; -plegia paralysis; -phasia speech.
Hemiparesis/hemiplegia: one side; quadriplegia: four limbs.
Aphasia = absence of speech.
-malacia softening; -cele hernia; -lysis destruction.
Neurology vs psychiatry.

deeper.title: Why the meninges are called 'mothers'
deeper.html:
Mater is Latin for mother: the old anatomists saw these membranes as protecting the brain as a mother protects a child. Dura (hard) and pia (tender) describe their texture, and arachnoid describes the web-like middle layer. The names are a memory aid for their order and properties.

Source: the lecture's meninges slides.

deeper.title: Why myel/o has two meanings
deeper.html:
Myel/o comes from the Greek for marrow: the spinal cord was seen as the 'marrow' inside the vertebrae. So myelitis is spinal cord inflammation, but myeloma is a bone-marrow tumour. Context, and the other word parts, tell you which marrow is meant.

Source: the lecture's combining forms and matching exercise.

figure.caption: Three membranes and their spaces, from outside in. Schematic drawn for this site.

provenance.note: 7 - Medical Terminology Reproductive system FM1E 2025.pdf (Medical Terminology, Pr Hicham Benyoussef)

body.build_note: Built from the lecture slides. Slides that only show pictures are covered in outline. If your professor says something different, trust your professor.
exam_points: Perineum: between pubic symphysis and coccyx.
Testis: orch/o, orchid/o, test/i; penis: pen/i, phall/i.
Ovary: oophor/o, ovari/o; tube: salping/o; uterus: hyster/o, metr/o, uter/o; vagina: vagin/o, colp/o.
Uterine layers: perimetrium, myometrium, endometrium.
-gravida pregnant; -para give birth; nulligravida vs nullipara.
men/o menstruation: menarche, oligomenorrhea, menometrorrhagia.
mast/o breast: mastalgia, mastopexy (-pexy = fixation).
Orchiopexy fixes an undescended testis; oophorectomy removes an ovary.
Urologist: male genitourinary + female urinary; obstetrician: pregnancy and birth.

deeper.title: Why the uterus has three roots
deeper.html:
Hyster/o is Greek (hysterectomy), metr/o and metri/o are also Greek (endometrium, metrorrhagia), and uter/o is Latin (uterine). Each tends to appear in particular words, so recognising all three lets you decode surgery names, tissue layers and bleeding disorders alike.

Source: the lecture's structures and combining forms table.

deeper.title: Why -gravida and -para are counted separately
deeper.html:
A woman may have been pregnant without giving birth (miscarriage), so obstetric history records pregnancies (gravida) and births (para) separately. Nulligravida and nullipara are the starting points of that count.

Source: the lecture's word parts list.

figure.caption: Organs and their combining forms. Schematic drawn for this site.

provenance.note: 2 - Medical Terminology Respiratory FM1E 2026.pdf (Medical Terminology, Pr Hicham Benyoussef)

body.build_note: Built from the lecture slides. Slides that only show pictures are covered in outline. If your professor says something different, trust your professor.
exam_points: nas/o, rhin/o nose; laryng/o larynx; pharyng/o throat; trache/o trachea; bronch/o bronchus.
pneum/o, pneumon/o, pulmon/o lung; pleur/o pleura; phon/o voice; ox/o oxygen; capn CO₂.
-pnea breathing: eupnea, apnea, bradypnea (< 10), tachypnea (> 20).
Cheyne-Stokes: alternating fast and slow/apnoea, near death.
Aphonia = no voice; dysphonia = difficult speech.
Hypoxemia = low O₂ in blood; hypercapnia = high CO₂.
-thorax: pneumothorax (air), haemothorax (blood), pyothorax (pus).
-ectasis: bronchiectasis (dilation), atelectasis (incomplete expansion).
Croup: barking cough and stridor; pertussis: whooping cough.
Tracheotomy = incision; tracheostomy = stoma.
Otolaryngologist = ENT; pulmonologist = lung specialist.

deeper.title: Why so many -thorax words
deeper.html:
The suffix -thorax simply means chest, and the prefix or root tells you what has collected in the pleural space: air (pneumo-), blood (haemo-) or pus (pyo-). One pattern, three emergencies with different treatments. Recognising the pattern is the core skill the lecture trains.

Source: the lecture's pleura diseases slides.

deeper.title: Why -otomy and -ostomy are easy to confuse
deeper.html:
Both come from the Greek for cutting. -otomy is a cut into something (tracheotomy: an incision into the trachea); -ostomy creates a lasting opening, a stoma, to the body surface (tracheostomy: a hole through which a breathing tube passes). The one extra letter changes a procedure into a permanent opening.

Source: the lecture's word-building exercises.

provenance.note: 9 - Medical Terminology Integumentary system FM1E 2025.pdf (Medical Terminology, Pr Hicham Benyoussef)

body.build_note: Built from the lecture slides. Slides that only show pictures are covered in outline. If your professor says something different, trust your professor.
exam_points: Integument = to cover; skin is the largest organ.
Skin functions: protection, waterproofing, immune barrier, touch, vitamin D.
Skin: cutane/o, dermat/o, derm/o; sebum: seb/o; sweat: hidr/o; hair: pil/o; nail: onych/o, ungu/o.
hirsut/o hairy; kerat/o horny; melan/o black; myc/o fungus; rhytid/o wrinkle; urtic/o hives; xer/o dry.
Acne vulgaris: sebum overproduction, pustules.
Comedo: closed = whitehead; open = blackhead.
Seborrhea = excess sebum.
Macule: flat < 1 cm; papule: small raised; crust: dried serum.

deeper.title: Why blackheads are black
deeper.html:
A blackhead is not dirt: it is an open comedo whose sebum and keratin plug is exposed to air, where it oxidises and darkens. A whitehead is the same plug under a closed opening, so it stays pale. One word, comedo, covers both, and the open/closed distinction explains the colour.

Source: the lecture's pathology slide.

deeper.title: Why skin is part of immunity
deeper.html:
Intact skin is a physical barrier that most pathogens cannot cross, and sebum discourages bacterial growth on its surface. That is why the lecture calls intact skin the first line of defence of the immune system, and why burns and wounds carry such a risk of infection.

Source: the lecture's functions of the skin slide.
